title: Conditional Endorsement: Simulating How Adults with Different Skills Evaluate Canada's National AI Strategy
abstract: Canada's 2026 national AI strategy, AI for All, commits to free AI training for everyone and to expanding business AI adoption, yet it is difficult to anticipate whether these policies will reach adults with uneven skills and circumstances. We ask how adults with diverse skills might rate these policies on support, effectiveness, and personal benefit, how their skills and circumstances shape these evaluations, and what implementation conditions they raise. We built 3,200 generative agents from a weighted sample of the Programme for the International Assessment of Adult Competencies (PIAAC) Cycle 2 respondents, collected their ratings and explanations for 20 policies, and analyzed dialogues between agents with contrasting ratings. The agents supported nearly every policy but were far less confident that they would improve adult AI literacy or benefit them personally. This gap widened as digital technology use declined: agents modeled on adults who had never used a digital device still endorsed the policies but rarely expected to benefit. Agents traced the gap to participation costs, hard-to-exercise rights, and limited community control, and their dialogues specified these conditions rather than resolving disagreement. We describe this pattern as conditional endorsement and argue that AI literacy policy should be designed and evaluated for adults with the fewest digital skills.

title: How Artificial Intelligence Is Transforming Higher Education
abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI), particularly generative and agentic systems, is rapidly reshaping higher education. This article examines the main changes AI is introducing in teaching, learning, assessment, research, and institutional operations. Drawing on recent empirical studies and reviews up to 2026, it shows that AI enables personalised learning, faster feedback, and greater accessibility, while also creating serious risks of cognitive offloading, weakened critical thinking, academic integrity problems, and equity gaps. The central argument is that the value of AI depends less on the technology itself than on deliberate pedagogical design, AI literacy, and institutional policies that keep human judgement and independent thinking at the centre. The goal is to help universities and students use AI as a powerful support tool rather than as a substitute for learning.

title: Reclaiming Teacher Agency in AI Mediated Classrooms Exploring Professional Autonomy and Pedagogical Decision Making
abstract: The integration of artificial intelligence into education creates both opportunities and challenges for teachers’ professional autonomy and pedagogical decision-making. This study aims to examine how teachers maintain their agency, negotiate the use of AI, and make instructional decisions in AI-mediated classrooms. A qualitative approach with an exploratory case study design was employed involving 15 teachers in Bogor selected through purposive sampling. Data were collected through semi-structured interviews and documentation and analyzed using thematic analysis. The findings indicate that AI supports greater efficiency in lesson planning, material differentiation, and assessment; however, final instructional decisions remain grounded in teachers’ professional judgment, classroom context, and students’ needs. The study highlights the importance of AI literacy and adaptive school policies in strengthening teacher agency and promoting responsible AI use in education

title: Developing and Validating a Digital Competency Framework for Public Employees in Vietnam's Finance-Sector Public Service Institutions
abstract: Digital transformation has increased the demand for occupational digital competencies among public employees, particularly in public service institutions operating within Vietnam's finance sector. However, existing international digital competence frameworks may not adequately capture the specific professional requirements and institutional responsibilities of this workforce. This study aims to develop and empirically validate a context-specific digital competency framework by integrating competency theory, the European Digital Competence Framework (DigComp 2.2), and the OECD framework for digital talent and skills in the public sector. An exploratory sequential mixed-methods approach was employed, incorporating qualitative interviews with 18 participants, a pilot survey of 45 public employees, and a quantitative survey comprising 420 valid responses. The quantitative sample was divided into two independent subsamples of 210 observations for exploratory factor analysis (EFA) and confirmatory factor analysis (CFA), respectively. The proposed framework comprises seven competency dimensions measured by 28 indicators: information and data literacy, digital communication and collaboration, digital content creation, digital safety and ethics, digital problem solving, artificial intelligence literacy, and digital adaptability. title: Training Social Workers for the AI Era
abstract: The advancement of artificial intelligence (AI) is reshaping the landscape of social work practice and education. This chapter explores how the profession can prepare for this transformation through training and education while remaining rooted in its mission of equity and justice. This chapter begins by defining AI literacy and fluency for social workers and the need to engage with AI and ensure responsible use critically. Drawing on frameworks such as Boetto’s EPIC model and Ahn et al.’s AI literacy framework and using the Council on Social Work Education’s (CSWE) Educational Policy and Accreditation Standards (EPAS), this chapter illustrates how AI literacy aligns with core competencies and how social work education can embed these skills into curricula. Examples are provided to demonstrate how AI literacy can be integrated across micro, mezzo, and macro practice. This chapter also addresses the urgent need for upskilling and reskilling among current practitioners through accessible professional development opportunities, such as certificate programs, conferences, and community-based learning spaces. Together, training for the profession and education programs can build a future-ready social work profession that utilizes AI as a tool for innovation while safeguarding the values and commitments that define the field.

title: Continuing Education as Ethical Infrastructure: Informal AI Learning in Academic Librarianship
abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is transforming academic librarianship, requiring sustained ethical, evaluative, and instructional learning. Drawing on interviews with fourteen U.S. STEM academic librarians and scholarship on AI literacy and professional development, this paper examines how librarians develop AI competence through experimentation, peer networks, and personal knowledge management amid uneven institutional support. These conditions shift the costs of adaptation onto individual practitioners and raise concerns about equity, labor, and sustainability. The paper reframes continuing education as sociotechnical infrastructure for AI learning, identifies informal learning as structurally compelled labor, and proposes a role for library and information science (LIS) educators in designing ethical, collaborative, and sustained professional learning. Practice-based pathways, communities of practice, protected learning time, and institutional governance can support critical judgment as AI systems change.

title: Bridging the AI literacy gap: mixed-methods evidence from employers on workforce readiness and curriculum priorities
abstract: The rapid integration of artificial intelligence (AI) in the workplace has widened the gap between what universities teach and what employers expect of new hires. This study examines that gap through a mixed-methods research-to-practice design grounded in employer perspectives. Three objectives guided the work: (a) identify gaps between undergraduate AI preparation and workplace requirements, (b) develop a workforce-informed AI competency framework from documented industry needs, and (c) identify workforce-driven priorities for an AI literacy curriculum. Data were collected in four sequential phases: a structured narrative review ( n = 56), industry focus groups and interviews ( n = 13), survey instrument development, and a convenience sample of predominantly U.S. employers recruited through professional networks ( n = 110). Open-ended survey responses were analyzed through hybrid inductive-deductive thematic analysis. Findings indicated that employer-defined AI readiness is fundamentally socio-technical: task-specific prompting and tool fluency must be coupled with professional communication, collaboration, human oversight, and judgment, soft skills that employers rated as highly as technical AI competencies. Employers also perceived recent graduates as underprepared, particularly in AI output verification and AI ethics. abstract: BACKGROUND The transition from promising artificial intelligence (AI) models to improvements in routine clinical care remains limited, particularly in low- and middle-income countries (LMICs). An important barrier to clinical AI adoption in LMICs is limited workforce preparation. Evaluations of AI training programs targeting health workforces in LMICs also remain limited. OBJECTIVE To describe the AI for Global Health course, including course structure, participant reactions, self-reported knowledge, and attitudes toward AI. METHODS Partners In Health (PIH) and the University of Global Health Equity offered five two-hour synchronous online sessions to 38 participants across two cohorts. title: The Experience Advantage: Age-Inclusive AI Upskilling for the Longevity Workforce
abstract: Workers aged 55 and older now make up nearly a quarter of the U.S. workforce, yet they are frequently left out of the AI capability-building reshaping organizations. This article synthesizes recent AARP survey data, early labor market evidence on generative AI, peer-reviewed research on age stereotypes, age-diversity climate, job design, and older adults' learning, and documented organizational cases. It finds that older workers are increasingly familiar with AI and interested in learning to use it, but that a large gap separates interest from training received, that age stereotypes about technology persist, and that AI-enabled hiring tools have created new legal exposure for age discrimination. Early evidence suggests that AI's employment effects have so far fallen most heavily on young entry-level workers rather than experienced ones. The article proposes five evidence-based responses: age-inclusive AI training design, bias-proofed hiring and AI tools, career conversations at every age, mutual mentoring in multigenerational teams, and flexible, phased work with structured knowledge transfer. It concludes with three long-term capabilities for sustaining an age-inclusive AI workforce.

title: The Future of Beekeeping – An AI-driven Business Strategy for Sustainability
abstract: The future of beekeeping is more dependent on the industry’s ability to harness technology to ensure sustainability. The conventional methods of managing a hive are clearly not adequate, given the steady decline of pollinator species due to global warming and diseases. This paper will shed light on the role of AI technology and the sustainability of beekeeping, which will result in increased efficiency at work, along with increased profits, especially among small and medium-scale companies in the agricultural sector. The three distinct strands of inference based on the mixed methods design are case studies of AI-enabled apiaries, econometric modeling of return on investment tied to the adoption of AI, and the design of a strategic framework based on conducted interviews with more than 50 stakeholders, such as bee farmers, agritech developers, and policy advisors. From here, a framework is generated that integrates AI tools such as convolutional neural networks – Roboflow3, NLP, and IoT-based systems with the principles of the circular economy. In the first place, it adds to the literature on sustainability and AI by advancing a new sustainability framework for AI, which bridges technology capabilities and business models to enable scalability and real-time bee hive surveillance and detection. title: The Digital Fossil of Deliberation: A Human-Centered Architecture for AI Governance and Decision Accountability
abstract: Enterprise artificial intelligence governance in higher education and the public sector effectively controls data access and model safety, yet leaves a critical accountability gap at the point of decision: proving that a human reviewer actively evaluated, modified, and authorized an AI-assisted output before execution. This whitepaper introduces the Digital Fossil of Deliberation, a human-centered governance framework and technical reference architecture built on standard enterprise productivity and compliance platforms. By separating unedited AI drafts (State A) from human-validated outputs (State B) through a two-stage review gate, recording W3C PROV-O provenance metadata alongside SHA-256 cryptographic hashes, and isolating restricted personally identifiable information (PII) under scheduled retention purges, institutions can satisfy administrative fairness standards and British Columbia FOIPPA statutory obligations (Sections 28, 30, 31, and 69) without retaining sensitive records indefinitely.

abstract: The rapid digital transformation of the Mozambican public sector has been accompanied by growing investment in artificial intelligence (AI) enabled cybersecurity systems, including semi-autonomous platforms for threat detection and response. title: Studying AI Act Mentions: A first look at the impact of the European Union's AI regulation on Hugging Face
abstract: The European Union's Artificial Intelligence Act (AI Act) entered into force in August 2024, and its obligations apply in stages. Obligations for providers of general-purpose AI models have applied since August 2025, and transparency rules since August 2026. These obligations affect developers who share and deploy models and applications on public platforms such as Hugging Face (HF), the largest platform for distributing AI artifacts. However, little is known about how practitioners respond to the regulation in practice. To address this gap, we conducted an empirical study of explicit references to the AI Act on HF. We collected over five million records, including repository cards, discussions, and commits from Models, Datasets, and Spaces, and identified over 1,500 records that explicitly mention the Act. Two coders manually labeled these records using a primarily closed coding approach, and we analyzed the resulting categories per source. We find that explicit references to the AI Act remain rare across all repository types. Repository cards mainly contain claims of compliance and responsibility, like ensuring compliance or assigning responsibility to downstream users, and some claim that the Act does not apply because the model is not a general-purpose AI model. Discussions are used to report alleged violations of the Act, while commits mainly update artifacts that support compliance. title: Honest Brokers in AI Regulation: How Public Comments Introduce Evidence to Regulators
abstract: The regulation of Artificial Intelligence is susceptible to various forms of capture by industry actors that hold undue influence over the policymaking process, due in part to their information advantage in developing these technologies. In the following paper, we investigate the roles of public commenters in providing evidence to potential regulation in the USA. We build a corpus of 40 potential regulations, and 2,664 public comments submitted by a variety of stakeholders. We computationally process these texts to extract evidence meant to inform regulators, in the form of formal citations and informal references. We find significant differences in the type and amount of evidence supplied: Holding comment length constant, business commenters introduce altogether less evidence, and government, university, and civil society commenters provide significantly more research and legal sources. The publication status of cited research is nearly evenly split, with preprints and peer-reviewed articles being introduced by commenters of all types. We further explore patterns of self-citation and find that while it is prevalent amongst all groups, a small cluster of organizations account for over half of all self-citations in our corpus. Our findings complicate a narrative that public comments alone are means to information capture. We interpret these results in terms of the role that commenters attempt to play in the policymaking process-being either an Issue Advocate or an Honest Broke
authors: Sarah Tran, Anna-Maria Gueorguieva, Eva Maxfield Brown, Nicholas Weber

title: AI Regulations
abstract: This chapter examines the rapidly evolving global AI regulatory landscape and explores how governments around the world are developing legal and regulatory frameworks to govern the use of artificial intelligence. It reviews major AI-related laws and regulations across key jurisdictions, including the United States, the European Union, China, and other emerging regulatory regions, and analyzes the different approaches they have adopted to balance innovation, safety, accountability, and public trust. The chapter provides a detailed examination of the EU AI Act, including its risk-based classification framework, compliance obligations, General-Purpose AI (GPAI) requirements, and treatment of open-source AI systems. It also discusses common regulatory themes, emerging trends, and the practical implications for organizations developing, deploying, or using AI systems in a global operating environment. By understanding the regulatory landscape, organizations can better anticipate compliance requirements and align their AI governance programs with evolving legal expectations.

title: AI Regulation in Latin America
abstract: This article examines the normative instruments regulating artificial intelligence in ten Latin American countries, based on a systematic documentary survey conducted through August 2026. The mapping reveals the predominance of strategic plans, guidelines, and administrative acts, while comprehensive statutory frameworks remain under legislative consideration. The region is undergoing a gradual institutionalisation, marked by asymmetries and differing speeds of normative maturation.

title: Constructing the Risks of AI Regulation: Russian Media Discourse on the EU AI Act
abstract: This article examines the social dimension of technology adoption and development. Based on Russian media coverage of one of the stages in the adoption of the EU AI Act in June 2023, it analyzes the interpretive flexibility of technology - a situation in which a technology has not yet acquired a fixed evaluation, and this evaluation is being shaped through negotiations. The theoretical framework is the social construction of technology (SCOT), while the analysis of empirical material draws on the discourse theory of E. Laclau and Ch. Mouffe. The analysis shows that this particular stage of adopting AI regulation in the Europe reveals the heterogeneity of positions within the Union: the stance of the governing bodies (the European Commission, which approved this stage) - protecting end-users from potential risks of the new technology; the stance of business - advocating for freer development of AI systems; and the deep involvement of American technology corporations in the negotiation process. The Russian position is presented as more homogeneous; nevertheless, there is a call to accelerate the implementation of Russia’s own regulatory system, with particular attention to the development of material infrastructure.

abstract: 이 글은 인공지능기본법의 시행에 따라 기존 금융·개인정보·신용정보 규제와 인공지능 규제가 동일한 사업자·행위·데이터 및 위험에 중첩적으로 적용되는 경우, 규제의 기능적 병존과 실질적 중복·이중규제를 구별하고, 그에 따른 규제준수비용이 시장의 경쟁조건에 미칠 수 있는 영향을 평가하기 위한 규범적 판단모델을 제안한다. 특히 복수의 법률과 감독기관이 동일한 위험에 대하여 유사한 평가·검증·보고 및 자료제출 의무를 반복적으로 부과하는 경우, 그로 인한 증분 준수비용의 고정성·회수가능성·비대칭성이 시장진입과 경쟁능력에 어떠한 영향을 미치는지를 법적으로 판단할 수 있는 분석구조를 정립하는 데 목적이 있다. 이를 위하여 본 연구는 법적 의무를 개별 규제단위로 분해하고, 동일 행위·데이터·위험·통제수단·자료제출 및 평가·검증의 반복 여부를 확인하는 6요소 테스트를 제시한다. 다만 규제의무의 중복이 곧바로 경쟁제한성을 의미하는 것은 아니므로, 규제중복의 식별, 증분 준수비용의 분석, 경쟁조건에 대한 영향평가 및 규제대안의 선택을 구별되는 판단단계로 구성한다. 이러한 분석구조의 이론적 기초로서 Macaulay의 Law in Action, Becker의 비용과 경제적 유인에 관한 분석, Carstensen의 시장구조와 경쟁과정에 관한 논의 및 Habermas의 절차적 정당성 이론을 각각의 설명영역에 따라 재구성한다. 이를 통하여 실제 준수행위의 확인, 비용과 유인의 변화, 시장경쟁에 대한 영향 및 규제수단 선택의 법적 정당성을 연결하는 규범적 분석틀을 제안한다. 나아가 본 연구는 개인정보보호·금융안정·금융소비자보호 및 인공지능 안전성이라는 정당한 공익적 보호수준을 유지하면서 불필요한 규제중복과 경쟁제한적 비용을 최소화하는 규제수단의 선택원리를 ‘억제된 최적’으로 개념화한다. 이에 기초하여 동일 위험에 대한 기존 평가의 상호인정(One Risk–One Assessment), 동일 자료의 단일제출 및 복수 감독목적에의 활용(One Data–One Submission–Multiple Regulatory Uses), 잔여위험에 대한 보완평가 및 위험·기능·시장영향에 따른 차등규제를 제도적 대안으로 제시한다. 본 연구는 금융 AI 시장의 경쟁제한 효과를 실증적으로 확정하기보다, 향후 법집행 및 시장자료를 통하여 그 효과를 검증할 수 있는 법적 판단기준과 규제체계의 재설계 방향을 제시한다는 점에서 의의를 가진다.

title: Studying AI Act Mentions: A first look at the impact of the European Union's AI regulation on Hugging Face
abstract: The European Union's Artificial Intelligence Act (AI Act) entered into force in August 2024, and its obligations apply in stages. Obligations for providers of general-purpose AI models have applied since August 2025, and transparency rules since August 2026. These obligations affect developers who share and deploy models and applications on public platforms such as Hugging Face (HF), the largest platform for distributing AI artifacts. However, little is known about how practitioners respond to the regulation in practice. To address this gap, we conducted an empirical study of explicit references to the AI Act on HF. We collected over five million records, including repository cards, discussions, and commits from Models, Datasets, and Spaces, and identified over 1,500 records that explicitly mention the Act. Two coders manually labeled these records using a primarily closed coding approach, and we analyzed the resulting categories per source. We find that explicit references to the AI Act remain rare across all repository types. Repository cards mainly contain claims of compliance and responsibility, like ensuring compliance or assigning responsibility to downstream users, and some claim that the Act does not apply because the model is not a general-purpose AI model. Discussions are used to report alleged violations of the Act, while commits mainly update artifacts that support compliance. title: Risk-Aware AI Procurement in the U.S. Public Sector: Stochastic Optimization and Technology Governance
abstract: Public institutions acquire artificial intelligence (AI) services under established procurement, appropriation, and governance requirements, while commercial offers often state a rate and leave the quantity to later use. Executive leaders, procurement officers, financial authorities, and governance professionals need coordinated decision support so that a required review, a funding figure, and a management control are considered together. The objective is to give these decision-makers transparent, comparable financial estimates for AI service arrangements under uncertain demand. Operational controls and optimization are complementary parts of the proposed solution. The framework maps the reviewed rules onto subscription, consumption-based, prepaid-credit, and hybrid arrangements and labels each step as a legal requirement, a point the reviewed sources do not settle, or a recommended management practice. Ceilings, quotas, usage alerts, incremental funding, and named human approval are recommended practices, not Texas mandates. The proposed governance-constrained, riskaware decision optimization framework supports executive and institutional decision-making under uncertain AI consumption, financial exposure, and public-sector procurement requirements, while preserving human oversight and legally authorized decision authority. title: Shadow AI to Institutional Governance: A Lifecycle Framework for Generative AI in Scholarly Communication
abstract: Although the integration of Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) tools in academic research has accelerated, institutional governance frameworks remain rare. The reliance of many researchers on unmonitored, consumer-grade AI tools creates serious risks, such as fabricated citations, data breaches and loss of research context. Using a Design Science Research (DSR) approach, this study addresses this institutional governance gap. Following PRISMA 2020, we analyzed 41 peer-reviewed papers spanning 2020 to 2026, identifying a taxonomy of five AI adoption patterns. We developed the Lifecycle Governance Framework (LGF) with an 8×4 risk matrix across eight research stages and tested 22 commercial and open-source AI tools. Results indicated that no platform achieved full governance. Most governed only isolated stages, even for well-funded platforms, suggesting a gap in the current market rather than a resource constraint. The analysis found five issues: (1) tools lose context between research steps, (2) user logins are not secure, (3) human review is not required, (4) records of AI use are missing and (5) poorer universities cannot afford the cost. To solve these issues, we propose a clear research plan, a step-by-step guide and a working system design for university libraries and Information Technology (IT) departments to control AI safely.
authors: Asma Iman Kouachi, Abla Hedhoud, Abderraouf Bouferrouk

title: Fairness Theatre: Evaluating Post-Hoc Fairness Interventions in Vendor-Controlled Early Warning Systems
abstract: Public institutions increasingly procure AI systems whose design they cannot inspect or change. In higher education, proprietary Early Warning Systems (EWS) leave colleges with few options beyond adjusting model outputs to address inequity. This raises a CSCW question: how is fairness work coordinated among vendors, institutions, advisors, and students with unequal power to change these systems? Using student records from a public college in Ontario, Canada, we evaluate six post-hoc fairness interventions on a research EWS under simulated procurement constraints. We compare fairness, accuracy, and demographic disparities, introducing error-type profiling to trace how interventions redistribute false positives and false negatives. Interventions redistributed disparities without consistently reducing them. Two implementations favoured already-advantaged groups because they used group size to define disadvantage; small, marginalized groups remained poorly served. These findings show how procurement constraints and implementation choices shape the possibilities for fairness work. We call the resulting condition fairness theatre : dashboard metrics converge while groups’ error burdens persist or worsen.
authors: Kelly McConvey, Angelina Zhai, Rebecca Li, Shion Guha

title: Artificial Intelligence & The United States Federal Government: A Policy Analysis of Governance, Private Sector Participation, and Public Value Across Administrations
abstract: Artificial intelligence is no longer an experimental idea in Washington; it has entered everyday federal administration. Commercial vendors build the underlying models and data centers, while federal agencies act as buyers, users, and regulators. This paper examines how the federal government adopts AI, how private vendors shape that process, and how policy approaches shifted between the Biden and Trump administrations. While the Biden administration emphasized civil rights, risk mitigation, and structured safeguards (Executive Order 14110; OMB M-24-10), the Trump administration shifted the focus toward rapid deployment, regulatory relief, and commercial competitiveness (Executive Order 14179; OMB M-25-21). Drawing on public administration concepts like the principal-agent dilemma, vendor lock-in, and administrative burden, this study reviews real deployments across payment integrity, clinical documentation, drug review, and national security. The central lesson is that buying commercial software does not automatically create public value. To build an AI policy that supports both ordinary citizens and private enterprise, the federal government needs in-house technical capacity, open procurement standards to prevent vendor monopolies, practical testing based on real staff workflows, and clear administrative due process for the public.

title: Artificial Intelligence and the Socialist Rule-of-Law State in Vietnam: Rethinking the Exercise and Control of Public Power
abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly entering public administration and governmental decision-making, expanding state capacity while raising new questions about the exercise and control of public power. This article examines these questions from the perspective of Vietnam's socialist rule-of-law State. It argues that AI is not a new source or autonomous subject of state power, but a technological condition through which legally constituted public authority may increasingly be exercised. The article develops the concept of the AI-mediated exercise of public power, referring to situations in which AI materially shapes the informational, analytical, procedural, or decisional processes through which public authorities make consequential decisions. Building on people's sovereignty, legality, state-power control, and accountability, it advances an Extension Thesis: when AI materially mediates public authority, effective control of state power must extend to the data, algorithms, AI systems, and human–AI arrangements through which that authority is exercised. The article further develops meaningful human authority and a public-power extension of existing AI impact-assessment arrangements. It concludes that AI-enabled modernization requires corresponding modernization of the institutions through which public power is authorized, exercised, controlled, and held accountable to the People.

title: GOVERNING TECHNOLOGICAL CONVERGENCE Legal Ethical and Regulatory Frameworks for Neural Data Organoid Intelligence and Autonomous Systems
abstract: This monograph presents a comprehensive framework for the convergent governance of neuroscience, artificial intelligence, and biotechnology. It addresses the challenges of neural interfaces, organoid intelligence, and autonomous systems through six foundational concepts. Neural sovereignty establishes robust rights over cognitive processes with narrow medical exceptions. The framework protects inferred neural data from algorithmic exploitation and proposes defensive cognitive friction, utilizing measurable delays to secure brain-computer interfaces. For organoid intelligence, it introduces a donor withdrawal protocol based on best technological efforts, acknowledging the limits of machine unlearning. Additionally, it advances dynamic risk classification for public sector AI and algorithmic impact assessments to prevent disparate impacts. Tackling extraterritorial enforcement to combat regulatory arbitrage, the book provides model legislation and impact checklists, equipping policymakers with actionable tools to protect human dignity and cognitive liberty.

title: Decoding Moral Vulnerability in AI Environments:A Case Study of Algorithmic Governance and Policy Implications
abstract: Purpose: This paper explores the hidden ethical costs of AI deployment in professional settings, specifically the induction of “moral vulnerability.” The overarching purpose is to provide policymakers and executives with actionable governance principles to ensure that AI-driven efficiency does not compromise human dignity, professional ethics, and sustainable digital transformation. Methodology: This paper utilizes a qualitative case study methodology, examining the UnitedHealthcare “nH Predict” AI algorithm failure. Rigor is established through the triangulation of secondary data, including the 2024 U.S. Senate Permanent Subcommittee on Investigations report, federal class-action litigation dockets, and investigative journalism. Findings: The implementation of AI without structural ethical guardrails actively disrupts organizational ethics through four interlocking dynamics: (1) impaired moral agency, (2) psychological moral distortion (responsibility displacement), (3) structural moral constraints tied to performance metrics, and (4) moral identity instability among professional staff. Originality: This paper introduces the novel conceptual lens of “Moral Vulnerability” to explain algorithmic failures. It moves beyond traditional analyses of technical algorithmic bias to focus on the psychological and structural degradation of the human-in-the-loop. Practical implications: Tailored for executives and policymakers, particularly those guiding initiatives like Oman Vision 2040

title: Strengthening Disability Rights Protections in The Digital Age Through Islamic Justice
abstract: Background/Introduction: Digital public services can expand access for persons with disabilities, but inaccessible design and automated decisions can create barriers. Research Objectives: This study assesses Indonesian regulations protecting disability rights in digital public services and proposes reforms informed by Islamic justice. Methodology: This normative legal study used statutory and conceptual approaches, drawing on responsive law theory and the principle of al-‘adl. Results: The provisions examined establish safeguards for accessibility, reasonable accommodation, disability participation, and automated decision-making. More specific rules are needed to clarify providers’ responsibilities for testing accessibility and addressing barriers throughout service delivery. Unique Contribution: The study proposes a framework combining universal design and reasonable accommodation, participation by individuals with disabilities, and algorithmic impact assessment with an accessible objection mechanism. Conclusion: The principle of al-‘adl makes equal access a measure of regulatory adequacy, from obtaining information and completing procedures to lodging objections. Recommendations: Future research should involve persons with disabilities and service providers in testing the framework, with a focus on access barriers and on how objections to automated decisions are handled.

title: Designing AI at the Rural Edge: A Micro-Social Venture Framework for Community-Led Digital Innovation
abstract: Generative and other AI-enabled technologies are accessible to small organisations, yet human–AI interaction (HAI) design guidance focuses on relatively direct user–system interaction. Rural HCI, community-centred design, participatory AI, digital inclusion, and social-enterprise research show that AI use is socially and organisationally situated. This late-breaking work develops the Micro-Social Venture (MSV) Framework through integrative conceptual synthesis of 55 selected sources. The framework connects six dimensions: Place, Community Agency, Organisational Mediation, Digital and AI Capability, Resource Conditions, and Governance and Social Outcomes. Its distinctive contribution is to treat the social venture as part of HAI itself: a community-embedded socio-technical intermediary through which AI is encountered, adapted, governed, and potentially refused. Five design propositions address place, collective agency, resource asymmetry, negotiated trust, and community stewardship. The framework is generative rather than predictive, offering HCI a diagnostic lens for examining community-embedded AI at geographic, organisational, infrastructural, and participatory edges.

title: Co-creating principles for human–AI collaboration: A participatory approach to organizational GenAI integration
abstract: This paper examines how participatory sociotechnical approach can support the organizational integration of generative AI (GenAI) in the creative work of a public service organization. Through an exploratory collaboration with the communications department of a Danish municipality, it investigates how employees collectively shape GenAI integration through participatory organizational inquiry and the co-creation of localized sociotechnical principles. The study contributes to design research by providing an empirical account of participatory GenAI integration, extending participatory AI scholarship towards organizational AI integration, and introducing Sociotechnical AI Reflection (STAIR) as a participatory sociotechnical reflection method supporting localized GenAI integration in organizational settings. The findings show that meaningful GenAI integration depends on situated, value-driven processes that reshape professional practice, collaborative work, and organizational learning. The paper contributes to ongoing discussions on how organizations can integrate GenAI in ways that align with professional values, organizational purpose, and creative agency.

title: Co‐evaluation of co‐production in mind and brain research: A dialogical approach
abstract: Co-production is increasingly used in mental and neurological health research, but less is known about how co-production itself can be co-evaluated. We conducted a study that aimed to systematically co-evaluate a 9-month project that co-produced strategic priorities and internal research-funding procedures for a new mind and brain research centre. The co-evaluation used a mixed-method design, including qualitative, quantitative, dialogical and post-implementation approaches, informed by an adapted RQ + 4 Co-Pro framework. The project involved 14 adult contributors who were also participants in the co-evaluation, including seven community partners alongside academic, clinical and research staff. Contributors across these roles also brought lived or living experience of mental-health difficulties, neurodivergence and marginalisation. Reflexive thematic analysis examined contributors' written reflections; perceived power was measured midway through the project and again at completion; findings were returned to the team for dialogical co-interpretation; and funding-panel members later reflected on implementation of the co-produced procedures. Thematic analysis generated six themes concerning time and resources, roles and identities, leadership and power, communication, institutional barriers and emotional labour and gains. title: Beyond the bright-dark binary of co-production: a paradox lens on co-assessment
abstract: While a substantial body of scholarship has emphasized the positive and ‘bright’ elements of co-production, more recent studies have drawn attention to its pitfalls and ‘dark side’. Although research has sought to bridge these contrasting perspectives by jointly examining benefits and drawbacks, it has largely maintained a binary distinction between them. Rather than treating these dimensions as separate or opposing, this study adopts a paradox lens to conceptualize them as inherently interconnected. Drawing on a case-study of co-assessment processes, we identify five paradoxes, with each pole reflecting elements typically associated with both the bright and dark sides of co-production. By reimagining the debate as inherently paradoxical, we move beyond binary approaches that privilege ‘bright’ (positive) aspects while minimizing ‘dark’ (negative) ones, advancing a more nuanced and realistic understanding of co-production. We show how such paradoxes are navigated, revealing coping strategies which vary across actors’ power dynamics and agency.

title: An Embedded Case Study on Co-production in Dental and Municipal Old Age Care
abstract: OBJECTIVES: The aim of this study was to identify and discuss different implementation strategies developed using a co-produced approach within a collaborative project between dental care and municipal care organisations. METHODS: This embedded, descriptive case study was based on 1 overall collaborative project between the Public Dental Care Service and four municipalities in the west of Sweden. Three cases from the overall project are analysed using intervention strategy components, all grounded in the Behaviour Change Taxonomy (version 1). RESULTS: Across the three cases, the collaborative project generated implementation strategies co-produced by dental and municipal care professionals. The strategies targeted specific behavioural determinants, such as knowledge, role clarity, environmental conditions and social support, using defined behaviour change techniques. Each case produced context-specific strategy components that were feasible to integrate into existing workflows within both dental and municipal care services. CONCLUSION: This article stresses the potential of co-production when addressing complex health care challenges. By involving various endusers, conducting thorough needs assessments and implementing tailored strategies, the project reported successfully developed oral health care processes for older adults in municipal settings. title: Dementia unmuted 2026: Evolving a community dementia festival through co-production, inclusion and lived experience
abstract: Background Dementia remains widely misunderstood and stigmatised, contributing to social isolation, exclusion, and reduced quality of life. Opportunities for meaningful, inclusive community engagement are often limited for people living with dementia and their carers. Co-production is increasingly recognised as an important approach to developing initiatives that are more accessible, inclusive, and responsive to lived experience. Aim Dementia Unmuted 2026 aimed to use accessible co-production methods to shape a more inclusive, equitable, and community-responsive festival for people living with dementia and their carers. Method A co-production survey explored participant preferences regarding location, accessibility, timing, and areas of interest. Findings directly informed festival design, resulting in events delivered across multiple community locations to maximise geographical inclusion. Weekday scheduling and ­volunteer transport supported accessibility. Welcoming, inclusive environments were prioritised throughout, and participants were offered opportunities for active contribution through performance, decoration, and personal storytelling. Programme content reflected participant interests, with a focus on music, literature, and outdoor activity.
